title: Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit
author: Leslie Marmon Silko
source: Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit: Essays on Native American Life Today (1996)
citation: Silko, Leslie Marmon. 'Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit.' Yellow Woman and a Beauty of the Spirit: Essays on Native American Life Today, Simon & Schuster, 1996, pp. 60–72.

sections.heading: Personal Narrative Essay (Complete Selection)

epigraph.quote: A beautiful person was someone whose actions brought harmony to the community, who was generous, modest, patient, and kind.

paragraphs: From the time I was a little girl growing up at Laguna Pueblo, I was aware that I was different. My skin was a shade lighter than my cousins'; my eyes were hazel, and my heritage was a mixture of Laguna Pueblo, Cherokee, Mexican, and white. In mainstream American society, difference is viewed with suspicion or condemnation. But among the traditional Laguna people, difference was understood as a natural, necessary manifestation of Creation.

My great-grandmother A'mooh was a full-blood Laguna woman whose memory stretched back to the old days before the railroad arrived in New Mexico in 1881. She had wrinkled brown skin and long white hair tied back with a yarn string. Every morning she washed my face in warm water, combed my tangled hair, and fed me hot atole—blue cornmeal mush. As she worked, she told stories: stories of the animals, stories of the drought, stories of Kochininako, the Yellow Woman.

In the Pueblo worldview, beauty was not an external aesthetic standard imposed by fashion magazines or cosmetic industries. Beauty was a quality of the spirit. A beautiful person was someone whose actions brought harmony to the community, who was generous, modest, patient, and kind. Physical appearance—whether someone was tall, short, stout, thin, scarred, or plain—was merely the outer shell of a living spirit.

In traditional Laguna culture, human beings were not viewed as superior masters of nature. We were one element in an interconnected web of kinship that included the red clay hills, the dry riverbed, the pinon trees, the deer, the rattlesnake, and the thunderclouds that gathered over Mount Taylor in late August.

When Protestant missionaries and government agents established bureau schools at Laguna in the late nineteenth century, they brought an entirely different system of values: hierarchy, competition, shame, and external beauty standards. Children were punished for speaking Keres, the Laguna language, and taught that Indian ways were backward and heathen.

Yet the old stories survived. Through centuries of Spanish conquest, Mexican dominance, and American assimilation policies, the Laguna people held onto their core truth: identity is not an isolated individual accomplishment; identity is rooted in memory, family, storytelling, and reverence for the earth. By returning to the spirit of Yellow Woman, we remember who we are.
